messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tailor
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 41

At twenty-four, she spends most of her days bent over fabric in a small alterations shop, guiding hems through the machine with steady hands that look calmer than she feels. She is a single woman from a Middle Eastern family, living with her parents and two younger siblings, and before the accident her life has a dependable rhythm. She works long hours as a tailor, taking in dresses, shortening sleeves, repairing seams that other people barely notice. She likes the precision of it, the way a crooked line can be corrected if she goes slowly enough. She is known in the shop as quiet, careful, and fast.

The collision happens on an ordinary afternoon nearly a year ago. She is in the front passenger seat while her cousin drives them home after picking up fabric from a wholesaler across town. They are talking about a wedding order that needs to be finished by the end of the week. She remembers the roll of traffic, the light changing, her cousin starting forward. Then she sees a truck coming too fast from the side. For a fraction of a second she thinks, with unusual clarity, *it is going to hit us*. She hears her own voice yell out. The sound of impact is violent and metallic, followed by shattering glass and the blunt force of her body thrown sideways against the seat belt. Everything narrows. She cannot tell where her legs are. There is smoke or dust in the air. She tastes blood. Her cousin is making a strange choking sound, and she is sure they are both about to die.

She does not lose consciousness, which in some ways makes it worse. She remembers the trapped feeling, the door bent inward, the smell of gasoline, people shouting outside. She keeps trying to move her hand toward her cousin and cannot. In the ambulance she is shaking uncontrollably, asking whether the car will explode, whether her cousin is alive, whether they are on fire. At the hospital she has bruised ribs, cuts along her arm, and a sprained ankle. Her cousin survives with more serious injuries. Family members tell her she is lucky. She nods because that is what she is supposed to feel.

In the first weeks after the crash, she expects the fear to fade once the bruises turn yellow and the stitches come out. Instead, the accident keeps happening in pieces. The flash of the truck returns when she closes her eyes to sleep. The sound of metal striking metal comes back when a tray drops in the kitchen or when someone slams the shop door. At night she jerks awake with her heart pounding, already crying before she fully knows why. Sometimes in the dream she is still trapped in the car; sometimes she sees her cousin dying beside her and wakes with crushing guilt, though she knows her cousin lived.

She stops riding in cars unless there is no other choice. If her father insists on driving her to work in bad weather, she sits rigidly, one hand braced against the door, scanning every intersection before they reach it. She gasps when another car comes too close. More than once she shouts “Watch out!” so suddenly that everyone in the car falls silent afterward. Eventually she starts taking longer routes on foot or paying for rides she cannot really afford, just to avoid sitting at a red light.

At the alterations shop, the work that once soothed her begins to feel fragile. The hum of the sewing machine can still calm her for a few minutes, but sudden noises snap her out of concentration. If a customer drops a bag or a delivery van backfires outside, her whole body startles. Her chest tightens and she feels pulled back to the passenger seat, breathless and trapped. She has to go to the restroom, lock the door, and wait until the dizziness passes. She becomes embarrassed by how often this happens. She worries the others notice she is no longer the same steady worker.

She also notices changes in herself at home. She is more irritable with her younger siblings, especially when they argue loudly. She keeps replaying small decisions from the day of the accident—if they had left ten minutes later, if she had insisted on another route, if she had driven instead. Part of her knows these thoughts lead nowhere, but they return anyway, persistent as a needle catching on the same thread. Her mother says she is distant now. This is true. She spends more time alone in her room, scrolling on her phone without absorbing anything, not wanting to answer questions about why she no longer visits relatives as often or why she refuses invitations that involve driving.

What troubles her most is that the world no longer feels casually safe. Before, danger belonged to news reports and other families’ tragedies. Now she studies every intersection like a threat. She sits near exits in public places. She listens for sirens. Even on calm days, her body seems to expect impact. She is exhausted by this vigilance, yet afraid of what will happen if she lets it go. At work she still threads needles, measures cuffs, and pins dresses for brides who speak excitedly about the future. She smiles, makes small adjustments, and does her job well enough. But underneath the careful routine, she is living as if the next collision is always only a second away.
